title: Blacksmith Hits $1 Billion Valuation as AI-Written Code Floods Testing Pipelines
excerpt: The two-year-old CI startup raised $66 million led by Sequoia, two months after a round that valued it at $550 million, as AI coding agents overwhelm the pipelines that must verify their work.
body:
• Blacksmith, a code-testing infrastructure startup founded in 2024, raised a $66 million Series C led by Sequoia Capital at a $1 billion valuation.
  • The round comes just two months after a $45 million Series B valued the company at $550 million; total funding is now about $125 million.
  • Annual recurring revenue has grown 17-fold this year and the platform has run more than 90 million CI jobs, as AI coding agents produce code faster than traditional pipelines can test it.
  • More than 10,000 companies now use Blacksmith, up from about 5,000 in August; the company plans to grow from about 40 staff to roughly 75 by year-end.

Blacksmith, a startup that runs the infrastructure companies use to test software before it ships, has been valued at $1 billion in a $66 million Series C round led by Sequoia Capital, the company announced on Wednesday, according to TechCrunch and Fortune.

The valuation has moved at unusual speed even by current AI-market standards. Blacksmith raised a $45 million Series B at a $550 million valuation just two months ago, led by Peak XV Partners, and a $10 million Series A a year ago valued it at $60 million. Total funding now stands at about $125 million for a company founded in 2024.

The Bottleneck Blacksmith Sells Into

Blacksmith sells continuous integration, or CI: the automated builds and tests every code change must pass before it can be merged and deployed. Co-founder and CEO Aditya Jayaprakash said the company was founded to make CI "less painful," arguing that most companies are struggling to keep up with the volume of CI they need to run — especially as AI agents write a growing share of the world's code.

"As agents write more of the world's software, the question that matters is whether it can be trusted."

— Aditya Jayaprakash, co-founder and CEO, Blacksmith

That is the commercial logic of the round. Coding agents from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google do not work office hours and do not limit themselves to one change at a time — but every change they produce still has to compile, pass tests and clear a pipeline before a human merges it. The testing layer, long treated as plumbing, has become the choke point, and Blacksmith's pitch is that it runs pipelines roughly twice as fast at about half the cost of standard GitHub Actions by running jobs on its own bare-metal machines in data centres around the world rather than rented cloud servers.

The Numbers Behind the Repricing

The growth figures explain why investors repriced the company twice in a year. Annual recurring revenue has grown 17-fold since the start of the year to what Jayaprakash describes as tens of millions of dollars, with the largest customers each spending more than $1 million a year. The customer count has doubled from about 5,000 companies in August to more than 10,000, including Mercury, Granola, Supabase, Handshake and LangChain. The platform has now run more than 90 million CI jobs.

Blacksmith was founded by Jayaprakash with Aayush Shah and Aditya Maru, who met as undergraduates at the University of Waterloo. Most of the new capital will go toward buying more computing capacity. The company has about 40 employees across San Francisco and New York and plans to reach around 75 by the end of the year.

What Could Slow It Down

The risks are the mirror image of the opportunity. Blacksmith competes with GitHub itself and with the cloud providers whose infrastructure it bypasses, all of which are investing in faster CI for AI-generated code. A valuation that has risen from $60 million to $1 billion in about a year also leaves little room for a growth stumble. For now, though, Blacksmith is the clearest example yet of a pattern defining this phase of the AI build-out: the money is flowing not only to the models that write code, but to the infrastructure that checks whether that code can be trusted.
